title: The Production Code
objective: After this level you can explain why Hollywood censored itself under the Production Code from 1934 and why a ratings system replaced it in 1968.
summary: To head off government censorship, Hollywood adopted the Production Code in 1930 and enforced it from 1934. Television, foreign films and a 1952 ruling weakened it; ratings replaced it in 1968.

cards.headline: From 1934 to 1968, Hollywood's own rulebook decided what you could see.
cards.body: No government office wrote it. The studios did, and they enforced it on themselves. Why would an industry that sold thrills sign up to cut them?

cards.headline: Censor yourself, or be censored
cards.body: In 1922 studio heads formed a trade group, the Motion Picture Producers and Distributors of America, and hired Will H. Hays to lead it. In 1930 it adopted the Production Code, drafted by Catholic publisher Martin Quigley and Jesuit priest Daniel Lord. The reason was self-defense: the code answered public outcry and the threat of government censorship. Better a rulebook you write than one written for you.

cards.headline: 1934: the code gets teeth
cards.body: The code needed enforcement. In 1934, as the Catholic Legion of Decency called for boycotts of films it found offensive, Hays set up the Production Code Administration under Joseph Breen. Members agreed to distribute only films it approved. The code forbade profanity, obscenity and graphic violence and crime, and insisted that good and evil never be confused.

cards.headline: Why it faded
cards.body: After World War II, television and foreign films, both outside the code's reach, undermined it. Then in 1952, in Burstyn v. Wilson, the Supreme Court ruled that films communicate ideas and couldn't face government censorship. The threat that made the code worth keeping was gone. In 1968 the code was replaced by the age-based rating system still used today.

cards.headline: The Code: explained
learned: 1930: studios adopt their own Production Code
Why: public outcry and the threat of government censorship
1934: an office approves every film before release
1952 ruling weakened it; ratings replaced it in 1968

questions.prompt: In 1968, Hollywood's Production Code was replaced by _____.

options.label: a government censorship board
options.rationale: The replacement came from the industry, not the government.

options.label: a ban on all foreign films
options.rationale: Foreign films helped weaken the code instead.

questions.explanation: In 1968 the Production Code gave way to the age-based rating system still used today.

questions.prompt: Why did Hollywood's studios write a censorship code for themselves?

options.label: A 1922 law ordered them to
options.rationale: The code was self-imposed; no law required it.

options.label: Ticket sales had stopped for every kind of film
options.rationale: The pressure was public outcry, not empty theaters.

options.label: To answer outcry and head off government censorship
Theaters refused to show sound films
options.rationale: Sound was a hit; censorship was the worry.

questions.explanation: The code was a self-imposed answer to public outcry and the threat of government censorship.

questions.prompt: With Level 42's majors in mind, why could the code office's approval make or break a film?

options.label: Only Congress could release a film without it
options.rationale: Congress didn't release films; the studios did.

options.label: The members who agreed to it controlled distribution
Its seal was needed to shoot in color
options.rationale: Color had nothing to do with approval.

options.label: Actors refused roles in unapproved films
options.rationale: The power lay with distribution, not actors.

questions.explanation: Members agreed to distribute only approved films, and the majors controlled distribution and the big theater chains.
